 Another six sunscreens sold in Australia fall short of SPF ratings
 The results from Kiwi advocacy group Consumer NZ echo Australian tests, which found many popular sunscreens fell short of their claims. 
 David Adams 
 Nov 3, 2026 
 2 min read 
 Share
 0 
 Prefer SmartCompany 
 A child applies sunscreen in Wollongong, Wednesday, June 11, 2025. Source: AAP Image/Melanie Russell 
 A further six sunscreens sold in Australia have fallen short of their advertised SPF in independent testing, with the Therapeutic Goods Administration closely considering the findings.
 Related Article Block Placeholder 
 Article ID: 347490 
 Stricter testing, lab reforms: TGA unveils tougher rules for sunscreen brands after SPF scandal
 David Adams 
 Testing conducted by Kiwi consumer advocacy organisation Consumer NZ found seven out of ten products did not meet their UV-protection claims, echoing prior tests by Australian group Choice .
 Of those to fall short, six are readily available to Australian consumers. They include:
 Marine Blue Dry Touch Sunscreen Lotion SPF50+ (tested at SPF 34);
 Sun Bum Mineral SPF50+ (tested at SPF 38);
 Beauty of Joseon Ginseng Sun Moist Sun Serum SPF50+ (tested at SPF 41);
 Invisible Zinc Sport Mineral Sunscreen Lotion SPF50+ (tested at SPF 42);
 Le Tan Coconut Sunscreen Lotion SPF50+ (tested at SPF 46); and
 Natio Sun Quick Dry Moisturising Sunscreen SPF50+ (tested at SPF 47).
 Cetaphil Sun Ultra Light Lotion SPF50+, which is also sold on Australian shelves, did meet its advertised claim.
 Commenting on the NZ results, Choice director of consumer impact Andy Kelly said all six of those products would still provide a high level of sun protection.

 Even so, “consumers should be able to trust that they’re getting the highest level of protection – as advertised on the bottle”, he said.
 The New Zealand testing results also show a higher baseline performance than many of the sunscreens initially tested by Choice, which found some sunscreens returned an SPF performance of only four.
 TGA addresses new tests
 Responding to the latest findings, the TGA said it is keeping a close eye on the Australian sunscreen market.
 Related Article Block Placeholder 
 Article ID: 322426 
 Timeline: More sunscreen brands pause sales after Choice’s SPF bombshell
 David Adams 
 “The TGA takes concerns about the performance and labelling of sunscreens seriously and will consider the reported results to determine whether further investigation or regulatory action in Australia is warranted,” the regulator said in a statement.
 The regulator reiterated that even if a sunscreen does not meet its maximum advertised rating, it can still provide better UV protection than no sunscreen at all.
 “Differences between an individual SPF test result and a labelled SPF claim do not, by themselves, mean a sunscreen provides no protection or is unsafe to use.”
 The TGA has also revealed plans to tighten Australian sunscreen testing criteria, which would require brands to provide testing data when their products are listed on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods, and require testing labs to meet stronger accreditation rules, among other reforms. 
 Sunscreen brands respond to NZ tests
 Responding to Consumer NZ, Natio said it was surprised by the findings, given its formula was tested by three laboratories, but the company declined to provide its full testing data.
 Distributors for Invisible Zinc similarly shared their surprise, and provided a 2021 lab report upholding its SPF50+ rating.
 The Farmers department store business, which sells Beauty of Joseon in New Zealand, offered 2023 test results to Consumer NZ, but has also temporarily withdrawn the product pending additional tests.
 Consumer NZ said Le Tan and Marine Blue did not respond to Consumer NZ emails, and Sun Bum did not respond to its requests for comment.
